lead: Gain margin and phase margin answer one practical question: how much can the loop gain rise, or how much extra phase lag can appear, before the closed loop becomes unstable? They are read from the open-loop frequency response, not from the closed-loop response. The idea is used in motor drives, power supplies, process loops and anywhere a controller must survive gain changes and delay. Both margins measure the distance of the open-loop plot from the critical point −1 + j0.
prereq: You need 4.3 Bode plots for logarithmic axes and 4.5 Nyquist plot and Nyquist stability criterion for encirclements, plus the stability ideas of Unit 3.

sections.h3: Crossover frequencies and the two margins

blocks.text: The open-loop frequency response G(jω)H(jω) is a complex number at each angular frequency ω in rad/s. The critical point is −1 + j0. If this point lies on the open-loop locus, the closed-loop characteristic equation 1 + G(jω)H(jω) = 0 has a root on the jω-axis, so the closed loop has a pole on the jω-axis. The closed loop is marginally stable only when all its other closed-loop poles are in the left half-plane. The two margins measure how far the locus stays from that point.

The gain crossover frequency ω<sub>gc</sub> is the frequency where the open-loop magnitude is one, that is |G(jω<sub>gc</sub>)H(jω<sub>gc</sub>)| = 1, or 0 dB. The phase crossover frequency ω<sub>pc</sub> is the frequency where the open-loop phase is −180°, that is ∠G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)H(jω<sub>pc</sub>) = −180°. A system may have more than one crossover; use the one that gives the smallest margin for design.

blocks.where: ω<sub>pc</sub> is the phase crossover frequency in rad/s, where ∠G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)H(jω<sub>pc</sub>) = −180°; |·| is magnitude; GM is in dB.
ω<sub>gc</sub> is the gain crossover frequency in rad/s, where |G(jω<sub>gc</sub>)H(jω<sub>gc</sub>)| = 1 (0 dB); PM is in degrees.

blocks.text: GM is the extra gain in dB that can be added at the phase crossover before the loop magnitude becomes one. If |G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)H(jω<sub>pc</sub>)| = 0.5, then GM = −20 log₁₀ 0.5 = 6.02 dB, so the gain can rise by a factor 10<sup>6.02/20</sup> = 2 before marginal stability. PM is the extra phase lag in degrees that can be added at the gain crossover before the phase reaches −180°. If the phase at ω<sub>gc</sub> is −150°, PM = 30°.
On a Bode plot, read GM at the phase crossover and PM at the gain crossover. The order matters. The steps below use the magnitude curve in dB and the phase curve in degrees.

items: Draw the 0 dB line on the magnitude plot. Find every frequency where the magnitude curve crosses 0 dB; take the relevant one as ω<sub>gc</sub>.
Draw the −180° line on the phase plot. Find every frequency where the phase curve crosses −180°; take the relevant one as ω<sub>pc</sub>.

At ω<sub>pc</sub>, read the magnitude in dB. GM is the negative of this value: GM = −M<sub>pc</sub>, where M<sub>pc</sub> = 20 log₁₀|G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)H(jω<sub>pc</sub>)| dB. A magnitude below 0 dB gives positive GM.
At ω<sub>gc</sub>, read the phase in degrees. PM is the phase value plus 180°. A phase above −180° gives positive PM.

On a Nyquist plot, let the negative real-axis crossing be at −a, where a>0. For a stable open loop, GM = 20 log₁₀(1/a) dB and the allowed gain factor is 1/a. PM is the angle from the negative real axis to the point where the locus crosses the unit circle: with phase φ at that crossing, PM = 180° + φ. The same sign rules apply.

blocks.text: For a stable minimum-phase open-loop system, positive GM and positive PM mean the closed loop is stable. Zero means marginal. Negative means unstable. If the open-loop system is itself unstable, these sign rules do not apply; count encirclements of −1 as in 4.5.

GM can be infinite. This happens when the phase never reaches −180° at any finite frequency, so there is no phase crossover. If a 0 dB crossing exists, PM is read there; otherwise PM is undefined even though GM may be infinite. The Nichols chart in 4.7 shows the same two distances on one grid.

PM is the better quick indicator of damping. A small PM means the closed-loop poles are close to the jω-axis, so a step input gives a large overshoot and a ringing response. The link between PM and overshoot is approximate; for a second-order system, the damping ratio and PM are related, and 4.2 gives the time-domain translation. GM protects against gain changes: ageing, temperature, a replaced sensor, or a higher plant gain can push the loop magnitude up. A common design target is PM of about 45° to 60° and GM of 6 dB or more, but the right values depend on the plant and the allowed overshoot.

The margins are properties of the open loop. They do not require solving for the closed-loop transfer function T(s). This is why they are used in tuning: measure or simulate G(jω)H(jω), read the two numbers, and adjust the controller. A loop with PM = 5° may still be stable in a simulation, but it will be sensitive to delay and gain error. A loop with large GM but small PM is not automatically safe: phase lag from a transport delay grows with frequency and can break the loop while the gain margin looks healthy.

figure.caption: Bode magnitude and phase for G(s)=50/(s(s+1)(s+10)). The gain crossover is near 2.10 rad/s and the phase crossover is at 3.16 rad/s; PM is read at the first and GM at the second.

spec.aria: Bode magnitude and phase curves for G(s)=50/(s(s+1)(s+10)); the magnitude crosses 0 dB near 2.10 rad/s and the phase crosses −180° at 3.16 rad/s.

examples.question: For G(s)=50/(s(s+1)(s+10)), find the gain crossover frequency, phase crossover frequency, gain margin and phase margin.
steps: Write the frequency response: G(jω)=50/[jω(1+jω)(10+jω)]. Its magnitude is |G(jω)|=50/[ω√(ω²+1)√(ω²+100)]. Its phase is ∠G(jω)=−90°−tan⁻¹(ω)−tan⁻¹(ω/10). Angles are in degrees.
Find ω<sub>pc</sub> from phase = −180°. Then tan⁻¹(ω)+tan⁻¹(ω/10)=90°. The tangent of the sum is infinite when 1−(ω)(ω/10)=0, so ω²=10 and ω<sub>pc</sub>=√10=3.16 rad/s.

Find ω<sub>gc</sub> by solving 50/[ω√(ω²+1)√(ω²+100)] = 1. At ω=2.10 rad/s, the denominator is 2.10×√(5.41)×√(104.41)=2.10×2.326×10.218=49.91, so the ratio is 50/49.91≈1.002. Thus ω<sub>gc</sub>≈2.10 rad/s.
examples.answer: ω<sub>gc</sub>≈2.10 rad/s, ω<sub>pc</sub>≈3.16 rad/s, GM≈6.85 dB, PM≈13.6°; the closed loop is stable but close to the margin.
examples.check:
import math
wpc = math.sqrt(10)
mag_pc = 50/(wpc*math.sqrt(wpc**2+1)*math.sqrt(wpc**2+100))
GM = -20*math.log10(mag_pc)
def mag(w):
    return 50/(w*math.sqrt(w*w+1)*math.sqrt(w*w+100))
lo, hi = 0.1, 10.0
for _ in range(100):
    mid = (lo+hi)/2
    if mag(mid) > 1:
        lo = mid
    else:
        hi = mid
wgc = (lo+hi)/2
phase = -90 - math.degrees(math.atan(wgc)) - math.degrees(math.atan(wgc/10))
PM = 180 + phase
print(f'{wgc:.2f}')
print(f'{wpc:.2f}')
print(f'{GM:.2f}')
print(f'{PM:.2f}')

traps: Do not swap the crossovers: GM uses |G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)| at the phase crossover; PM uses ∠G(jω<sub>gc</sub>) at the gain crossover.
GM is −20 log₁₀|G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)|. A positive dB value means the magnitude at ω<sub>pc</sub> is below 1. Using +20 log₁₀ gives the wrong sign.
PM is 180° + phase, not 180° − phase. A phase of −150° gives PM = +30°.
The sign rules GM positive and PM positive for stability apply to a stable minimum-phase open loop. For an open-loop unstable plant, use the Nyquist encirclement count in 4.5.
If the phase never reaches −180°, GM is infinite, not zero. Report PM normally.

quiz.a: The frequency ω<sub>gc</sub> where |G(jω<sub>gc</sub>)H(jω<sub>gc</sub>)| = 1, that is 0 dB.

quiz.q: Why does a positive GM mean the gain can increase before instability?
quiz.a: At ω<sub>pc</sub> the phase is already −180°. Increasing gain multiplies the magnitude. Marginal stability occurs when the magnitude reaches 1. GM is the dB rise needed, so the allowed factor is 10<sup>GM/20</sup>.

quiz.q: A loop has |G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)H(jω<sub>pc</sub>)| = 0.25 and ∠G(jω<sub>gc</sub>)H(jω<sub>gc</sub>) = −150°. Find GM and PM.
A loop has GM = 8 dB. By what factor can its gain increase?
Can a stable minimum-phase loop have infinite GM and finite PM? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes. If the phase never reaches −180° for finite ω, there is no phase crossover, so GM is infinite. The magnitude still crosses 0 dB at some ω<sub>gc</sub>, so PM = 180° + phase at that frequency is finite.

quiz.q: Why are margins read from the open-loop response rather than the closed-loop response?
quiz.a: Closed-loop stability is decided by 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0. The open-loop locus and its distance from −1 directly measure that. Reading T(jω) shows the closed-loop shape but does not directly give how much loop gain or phase can change before the characteristic equation reaches the jω-axis.

beyond: Not for the exam. Servo drive autotuning often measures the plant frequency response and sets the current-loop PM near 45° to 60°; power-supply compensation uses GM to survive input-voltage and load changes. Robust control replaces single-number margins with disk margins and μ-analysis because gain and phase can vary together. Search 'stability margins Bode', 'phase margin servo tuning', and 'disk margin robust control'.
